skills.name: Trade blocs: opportunities, implementation and limits

note.text: Regional integration can widen markets, support production links and coordinate some rules. Benefits depend on implementation, infrastructure and firms’ capabilities. Trade creation replaces a higher-cost domestic source with a lower-cost partner; trade diversion shifts purchases from an efficient non-member towards a less efficient member because of preferences. An agreement’s objectives are not proof that all barriers have disappeared.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to assess a regional trade proposal and calculate an invented within-region share. Builds on: forms of trade integration. Leads to: later trade case studies and development comparisons.

sections.heading: Explain the geography

Trade creation replaces a higher-cost domestic source with a lower-cost partner; trade diversion shifts purchases from an efficient non-member towards a less efficient member because of preferences. An agreement’s objectives are not proof that all barriers have disappeared.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: CEMAC provides a regional institutional example for Cameroon. The AfCFTA agreement seeks a wider African market and progressive liberalisation; its objectives do not mean identical implementation everywhere. In an invented regional record, within-region exports are {30} units out of total exports of {120}; the share is {30/120*100} per cent. These are not official statistics.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Separate an institution’s aim from evidence of results. Check internal and external costs before naming trade creation or diversion. For the stated within-region export share, divide within-region exports by all exports and multiply by {100}; use the same period and valuation basis.

cards.idea: Distinguish the features before applying them.
example: market enlargement: access to a wider potential customer base.
trade creation: replacement of higher-cost domestic production by a lower-cost partner supply.
trade diversion: a preference-induced shift from an efficient outside source to a less efficient partner.
implementation gap: a difference between agreed objectives and realised conditions.

cards.idea: Use the evidence in the example, not a place name alone.
example: An invented producer can seek customers in partner economies.
An invented model switches to a lower-cost partner source.
An invented tariff preference changes sourcing towards a higher-cost partner.
An agreement exists but a fictional border procedure still delays goods.

cards.idea: Explain how the process produces the stated effect.
example: Capabilities, competition and implementation affect results.
Compare the previous and new sources and their costs.
Preferences may alter the relative price of member and non-member supplies.
Institutions and actual practices must be assessed separately.
